title: Confident and Adaptive Generative Speech Recognition via Risk Control
claim: Fixed-size hypothesis sets waste computation and can hurt; adapting set size to input difficulty with risk control is better and guaranteed.
layout: 2 panels: left heatmap, right stacked top/bottom pipelines split by dashed line
description: The figure has two panels. Panel (a), labeled 'Motivating Example', is a heatmap. The x-axis is set size from 1 to 5 and the y-axis is sample index. The color bar runs from 0 (dark purple) to 1 (yellow) and shows WER. Red dashed lines split the samples into three groups: improving, flat, and degrading. The top group has a bright yellow-green gradient at set size 1. The middle group is a uniform dark blue. The bottom group is dark and streaky. Panel (b), labeled 'Method Illustration', is split by a thick dashed black line. The top half shows the standard generative error correction pipeline. A waveform goes into a green ASR Model box, then a yellow note listing a 5-best hypothesis set, then a purple LLM box, then the corrected text with a green checkmark. The bottom half shows the adaptive version. The ASR Model branches into a larger note for difficult inputs and a smaller note for easy inputs, and both feed the LLM. A risk-control guarantee formula, P(WER − WER_best ≤ α) ≥ 1 − δ, is shown at the output.
caption: (a) WER performance patterns across hypothesis set sizes over TedLium-3. Samples are grouped by monotonicity: samples that improve with more hypotheses (top), show consistent performance (middle), or degrade with more hypotheses (bottom). (b) Comparison of standard GER using fixed 5-hypothesis sets versus our adaptive GER that dynamically selects variable-sized hypothesis sets with risk control to bound relative performance degradation from the oracle.
abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems frequently produce transcription errors due to acoustic variability, which require post-processing correction methods. Recent approaches leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) for generative ASR error correction using N-best hypotheses but rely on fixed set sizes regardless of input complexity and do not provide performance guarantees. We propose an adaptive framework that dynamically determines the optimal number of hypotheses for each input using risk control. This mechanism leverages ASR confidence scores and applies Learn then test (LTT) to control the expected relative word error rate degradation compared to the best achievable performance for a given model and hypothesis set. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach provides theoretical guarantees with high-probability bounds while matching or exceeding fixed-size correction baselines and requiring fewer hypotheses on average, achieving substantial computational savings under diverse acoustic conditions.
